strengths: Well-motivated core insight that output lengths are inherently stochastic and should be modeled as distributions rather than point estimates
Theoretical analysis (Theorem 3.2) provides justification for heavy-tailed behavior with empirical validation showing 93.1% KS pass rate for log-t distribution

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across online/offline scenarios, multiple datasets (LMSYS, ShareGPT, Alpaca), and model scales (8B, 70B, plus 6 additional models) demonstrating strong and consistent improvements
Practical implementation with asynchronous prediction and dynamic batching addresses real deployment challenges; clear O(log n) complexity analysis
Strong empirical results with 2.31× per-token latency improvement for online serving and 1.42× throughput improvement for offline SDG
Thorough ablation studies validate design choices including distribution families and score computation methods
Good cross-model and cross-dataset generalization demonstrating robustness of the approach
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, particularly heatmaps showing superior request clustering
weaknesses: No empirical comparison with recent preemptive methods (TRAIL, ELIS, Wu et al. 2023). These SOTA approaches are dismissed on overhead grounds without measurement, representing a significant baseline gap for a scheduling paper

Assumption 3.1 (termination rate density f(p) ~ c·p^(α-1)) lacks rigorous justification. The intuitive motivation (JSON structures, detailed explanations) is hand-wavy and the leap to power-law decay is not formally proven
Effective termination rate (Eq. 16) assumes generation 'type' determined early contradicts context dependency in autoregressive generation; oversimplifies the actual decoding process

Prediction model achieves only 0.76 R² for σ parameter (controls tail behavior), but paper doesn't analyze sensitivity to this substantial prediction error or how prediction quality impacts scheduling

Training data collection requires 20 repeated generations per prompt (~900K samples) - expensive and difficult for practitioners to replicate on new models/domains. Appendix E acknowledges but offers no concrete solution

Multiple ad-hoc design choices lack sensitivity analysis: α=0.9 for CVaR (why this percentile?), β formula (Eq. 12) derivation missing, exponential decay parameters (γ=0.9, τ=30s) unjustified, 10k MC samples arbitrary
Generalization claims overstated: Table 2 shows TIE doesn't uniformly dominate LTR across conditions (e.g., Alpaca 70B), suggesting approach not universally superior despite narrative
Limited ablation scope: only 3 fixed ν values tested in sensitivity analysis; no systematic exploration of β, γ, τ parameters; no analysis of MC sample size impact
Theoretical-practice gap: Theorem 3.2 justifies power-law behavior but doesn't explain why 20 samples suffices for fitting or connect to hyperparameter choices
Comparison scope limited: only FCFS, SSJF, LTR baselines; recent prediction methods mentioned but not compared; alternative risk metrics not explored

strengths: Well-motivated core insight: distribution modeling correctly captures stochastic nature of LLM decoding vs. point estimates
Rigorous theoretical grounding: Theorem 3.2 provides formal justification for heavy-tailed output length distributions with empirical validation (93.1% log-t fit pass rate)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple scenarios (online/offline), three diverse datasets, nine models tested, extensive ablations (Tables 4-12), and cross-dataset/model generalization
Strong and consistent empirical results: 2.31× per-token latency improvement over SOTA, 1.42× throughput improvement; advantages hold across diverse settings
Practical engineering contribution: asynchronous prediction architecture elegantly addresses overhead through decoupled threads and dynamic batching
Honest limitations discussion: acknowledges training data requirements and provides sensitivity analyses showing TIE outperforms with only 1/6 of baseline training data
weaknesses: Incomplete treatment of preemptive scheduling: TRAIL comparison relegated to appendix (Table 11); at low-moderate load (≤40 RPS) TRAIL is competitive, suggesting TIE represents a trade-off rather than clear superiority—this deserves prominence

Significant training data requirement: requires 20 generations per prompt vs. point-estimate methods using single-pass production logs; limits practical deployment despite data efficiency improvements
Hyperparameter choices lack full justification: CVaR threshold α=0.9 has no ablation; adaptive β range [0.1, 0.5] appears ad-hoc; starvation decay parameters γ=0.9, τ=30s not systematically justified

Assumption 3.1 justification is informal: claim that termination rates follow f(p)~c·p^(α-1) motivated by examples (JSON, structured output) but lacks formal derivation; sensitivity to this assumption unexplored

Distribution fitting limited to single source: evaluation of log-t fitting uses primarily LMSYS-Chat-1M; testing across completely different domains (math, code-focused prompts) would strengthen generalization

Limited analysis of corner cases: scheduling overhead claims (4.26ms 'negligible' at 100 RPS) don't account for scaling at extreme concurrency; prediction batching bottlenecks at very high load unexplored
Important details relegated to appendix: TRAIL comparison, diagnostic statistics by prompt family, training hyperparameters; key trade-offs should be in main text
Some design choices lack deep investigation: fixed ν=3.5 across all prompts (dynamic ν marginally worse but unexplored); no exploration of prompt-specific parameters
